JMPR: Ethoxyquin
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Ethoxyquin (default residue definition covering parent compound)
Peer review (EFSA, 2010d) and MRL review (EFSA, 2013c): Cannot be allocated based on the available data
efsa_comments:
At EU level, the residue definition for plant and animal products set under Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 covers the parent compound only (default residue definition).
In the framework of the periodic review, JMPR was unable to agree on a residue definition as the metabolism study did not adequately identify the residues present on storage of post‐harvest treated pears and as the toxicological data were not sufficient.
The previous RD for risk assessment (plant products) established by JMPR in 2008 (Ethoxyquin multiplied by a factor of 2.5 to account for the metabolites/degradates MEQ, DHEQ and DHMEQ) is not confirmed.

EU: Reg. 396/2005: Maleic hydrazide
efsa_comments:
Residue definition for enforcement is the same in the EU and derived by the JMPR.
The residue definition for risk assessment for plants in the EU is maleic hydrazide (restricted to foliar treatment on root crops only).
The latest peer‐review (EFSA, 2025i) considered the additional toxicological data available on 3‐pyridazinone leading to a separate ADI for this metabolite (see Section 1.1.2). Therefore, the expression of the risk assessment residue definition in animal commodities was proposed.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Methoprene
No EU peer review and no MRL review
efsa_comments:
Residue definition for enforcement is the same in the EU and JMPR.
At EU level, no risk assessment residue definitions have been set since methoprene residue behaviour was never assessed in the EU.
Considering the log Pow, and the findings of animal metabolism/feeding studies, the modification of the residue definition, including the label (F) for fat‐soluble substances should be considered in the EU.
The residue definition of JMPR was based on metabolism studies in wheat (post‐harvest treatment), alfalfa and rice (both foliar application). No specific metabolism studies are available for fruits (post‐harvest treatment).

JMPR: Propiconazole
EU: Reg. 396/2005: Propiconazole (sum of isomers)
efsa_comments:
The EU residue definitions for risk assessment are currently provisional. It is noted that the available metabolism studies with propiconazole (which is a racemic mixture of four stereoisomers) do not investigate the impact of plant and livestock metabolism on the isomer ratio of propiconazole.
The JMPR residue definitions (based on common moiety) appear more comprehensive. However, the genotoxicity and the general toxicity of certain metabolites (CGA118244, CGA91304 and CGA118245) identified in plant and livestock metabolism studies covered by the common moiety residue definition are not adequately addressed.

JMPR: Buprofezin
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Buprofezin
Peer review (EFSA, 2025c): Buprofezin
efsa_comments:
EU: For plant and animal products, the default RD for MRL enforcement is applicable (i.e. parent compound only), as no EU uses/import tolerances for food commodities.
Metabolism studies in livestock were not evaluated in the recent peer review (EFSA, 2025c). In case an animal residue definition would become necessary, a re‐evaluation of the livestock metabolism studies and toxicological data on the pertinent metabolites to current standards would be required. For plant commodities, the residue definition derived in 2010 was proposed on provisional basis. In the framework of the renewal process (EFSA, 2025c), which was restricted to non‐food and non‐feed crops, data on metabolites of buprofezin that could be important for the consumer dietary risk assessment were not provided. Therefore, the residue definition for risk assessment was not established and no consumer risk assessment was finalised.
JMPR: The parent compound was considered a sufficient marker for MRL enforcement; for paddy rice, appropriate metabolism studies were not available to conclude on the appropriate residue definition (as paddy rice may take up metabolites from sediment/water systems, JMPR concluded that radio‐labelled metabolism studies on paddy rice and radio‐labelled degradation studies in water/sediment systems are needed to assess the appropriateness of the current residue definitions). The RD for RA for other plant products (except paddy rice) and for animal products is restricted to buprofezin.

The residue is fat soluble
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Etofenprox
The residue is fat soluble
efsa_comments:
The EU risk assessment residue definition for plant is wider, includes alpha‐CO. See also the consumer risk assessment.
The residue definition for risk assessment (animal products) is tentative, because the following data were not available in the MRL review:
–
metabolism studies in ruminants and poultry performed with the parent and the metabolite alpha‐CO;
–
a fully validated method for enforcement in kidney and liver;
–
storage stability studies investigating stability of etofenprox in eggs, milk and animal tissues others than liver.
Confirmatory data were requested under Regulation (EC) No 396/2005.
The RMS informed EFSA that the requested confirmatory data were submitted and were assessed in the renewal process. According to the RMS, a new metabolism study in laying hens and lactating goat with alpha‐CO (taking into account the metabolic behaviour of alpha‐CO and the lower toxicity compared to the parent compound) will be available for the renewal process.

JMPR: Pydiflumetofen
EU: Peer review (EFSA, 2019i): Pydiflumetofen
efsa_comments:
The EU approval process is still ongoing, and therefore, a final decision on the residue definitions has not yet been taken. Currently, the default residue definitions (Art. 18(1)(b)) are applicable for enforcement. The residue definitions proposed in the EFSA conclusion are comparable with the Codex residue definitions except for animal products (risk assessment). For animal products (all matrices), a provisional residue definition for risk assessment was proposed, which covers the parent compound and 2,4,6‐TCP.
Additional toxicological data for 2,4,6‐TCP requested during the peer review were submitted and assessed in 2024 by EFSA. However, the data were not sufficient to conclude on the genotoxic potential of 2,4,6‐TCP, and therefore, no definitive RD for RA for animal products could be proposed.
The EU residue definitions for primary crops were proposed to be applied also to rotational crops. Pydiflumetofen is a very persistent compound (DT50 = 8540 days EU value), the accumulation of residue and consequently the uptake from the soil cannot be disregarded (see also the general comment from the MRL assessment). The JMPR residue definition for animal products (risk assessment) for mammalian liver and kidney comprises TCP and an additional metabolite (relevant only for liver and kidney).

JMPR: Florpyrauxifen‐benzyl
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Florpyrauxifen‐benzyl
Peer review (EFSA, 2018b): Florpyrauxifen‐benzyl (cereals only)
efsa_comments:
Plants:
At JMPR level
, four crops were investigated in primary metabolism studies: cereals (wheat (foliar) and rice (various applications)), fruits (soil) and pulses and oilseed (foliar), using labels at [PY‐], [PH‐] and [BE‐] positions. For rice, foliar flooded, water injected and dry‐seeded scenarios were investigated.
Florpyrauxifen‐benzyl was extensively metabolised across all investigated crops, with X11966341 and X11438848 identified as the major metabolites in both free and conjugated forms. These metabolites were primarily observed in plant parts used as feed items, forage with X11966341 up to 47% TRR and X11438848 up to 17% TRR. In contrast, residues in seeds and wheat grains were minor (< 0.004 mg eq/kg).
In rice grain, residues exceeded 0.01 mg eq/kg in only one scenario, showing the same metabolic pattern as other plant parts: florpyrauxifen‐benzyl (max. 6% of TRRs), X11966341 and X11438848 each < 4% of TRRs. In apple metabolism studies, no transfer of residues to the plant was observed following soil treatment.
In the EU, similar metabolism studies on rice were available during peer review. Based on those studies, the residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment were derived for cereals only. In the expression of the RA‐RD, it was provisionally assumed that X11966341 is covered by the parent toxicity. JMPR has not considered necessary a RA‐RD, while for enforcement, similar residue definition for all plant commodities was derived. However, EFSA is of the opinion that additional metabolism studies in fruits via foliar application would be needed to confirm whether the metabolic pattern is similar. Currently, no CXLs for fruits are evaluated.
Animal: Similar metabolism studies were assessed at both JMPR and EU levels in poultry and goat. Most of the radioactivity was excreted (97% of TRRs), with only minimal amount found in animal tissues. In poultry, residues were less than 0.01 mg eq/kg. In ruminants, X11966341 (up to 25% TRRs) and X11438848 (up to 45% TRRs) were recovered only in kidney and liver, while the parent compound was never detected. In other tissues, residues were < 0.01 mg eq/kg, and no further identification was performed.
Based on these findings, the residue definition for enforcement was derived in the EU as florpyrauxifen‐benzyl by default, while at the JMPR level, two metabolites were included. For risk assessment, JMPR did not consider it necessary to propose a residue definition. It is highlighted that the use assessed under EU peer review did not trigger the livestock assessment.
